title: "The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press"
subtitle: "Throws that leave the quarterback's hand in about two seconds: what they are, how he picks one before the snap, and why every offense needs them"
description: "The quick passing game from the ground up: why it exists (beating pressure, staying on schedule, stretching the run game sideways), the rhythm throw, receiver leverage and the pre-snap read, the core concepts (slant-flat, stick, snag, spacing, speed out, double slants, hitch-seam), how a receiver beats press (release, stem, stack, break, catch point, double move), now and bubble screens, and why short, fast throws are the standard answer to press coverage and the blitz."
glossary:
  "Quick game": "Pass plays built to get the ball out in roughly 2.5 seconds or less: a short drop, short routes and a throw timed to the receiver's break. Used to beat pressure, stay ahead of the down and distance, and stretch the run game sideways."
  "Rhythm throw": "A pass thrown on the quarterback's last step of his drop, with no hitch or hesitation, so the ball arrives just as the receiver breaks."
  "Pre-snap read": "The quarterback's look at the defense's alignment before the snap (leverage, cushion, the safeties, the box) that tells him which side or which receiver a play should go to."
  "Leverage (inside / outside)": "Which side of a receiver a defender lines up on. Inside leverage protects the middle of the field and concedes routes toward the sideline; outside leverage protects the sideline and concedes routes inside."
  "Slant-flat": "A two-receiver quick concept: the outside receiver runs a slant and the inside receiver a flat route underneath it, so the one defender between them can't cover both. A high-low read."
  "Stick": "A three-receiver quick concept: one receiver runs to about six yards and settles facing the quarterback (the stick), one runs to the flat, and the outside receiver clears out deep. The quarterback reads the flat defender."
  "Snag": "A three-receiver triangle concept: the outside receiver settles at five or six yards just inside his alignment (the snag), the slot runs a corner route behind him and a back or tight end runs to the flat, so two defenders face three receivers at three depths."
  "Spacing": "A quick concept that spreads four or five receivers across the field at about the same depth (five or six yards), each settling in the gap between two zone defenders: a horizontal stretch of the whole underneath coverage."
  "Speed out": "A quick out route run at full speed with a rounded break toward the sideline, thrown before the receiver breaks, usually against a cornerback playing off and inside."
  "Double slants": "Two receivers on the same side both running slants, the inside one shallower and quicker, so their paths stack in front of the defenders."
  "Hitch-seam": "A two-receiver quick concept: the outside receiver runs a hitch and the inside receiver a seam straight up the field, a high-low read on the defender between them."
  "Release (vs press)": "A receiver's first moves off the line against a defender pressing him: footwork and hand-fighting that get him past the jam and onto his route without being knocked off it."
  "Stem": "The part of a route between the release and the break. The receiver uses its direction and speed to move the defender where he wants him before he breaks."
  "Stacking (a defender)": "Getting directly in front of a defender who is trailing in coverage, on his line, so he has to go through the receiver to reach the ball."
  "Contested catch": "A catch, or attempted catch, made with a defender close enough to touch or fight for the ball at the catch point."
  "Double move": "A route that fakes a common short route (a slant, a hitch, an out) to get the defender to jump it, then breaks a second time, usually deep."
  "Now screen": {def: "A wide receiver screen thrown the instant the ball is snapped: the receiver takes a step back and catches it, with a teammate blocking the nearest defender. Built to punish defenders playing far off.", aliases: ["Smoke screen", "Quick screen"]}
  "Bubble screen": "A screen to an inside receiver who drifts back and out toward the sideline (the 'bubble') and catches the ball on the move, behind blocks from the receivers outside him."

`````` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"}
import os
import logging
import shutil

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Polygon, RegularPolygon
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Patch

from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, routes as r, style
import gridiron.play as gp

# A firm quick-game throw travels roughly 22-26 yards a second; gridiron's default (18) is an average over
# all throws and makes a five-yard slant look slow. This only changes the setting inside this chapter.
gp.BALL_SPEED = 24.0

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
READ_GREEN = "#0f7a55"   # a darker step of the aqua highlight, for text and read lines on the light field
GREY = style.MUTED
LINE_D, OFF_BALL, GUN = -0.7, -1.5, -5.0


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- players and alignments
def O(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label or key)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line5():
    """The five offensive linemen, 1.6 yards apart (only the center is lettered)."""
    return [O(k, k, LINE_D, w, "C" if k == "C" else "") for k, w in
            (("LT", -3.2), ("LG", -1.6), ("C", 0.0), ("RG", 1.6), ("RT", 3.2))]


def spread(rb_w=-1.5, x_w=-15.0, h_w=-9.0, y_w=9.0, z_w=15.0):
    """11 personnel, shotgun 2x2. X and Z on the line (with the five linemen: seven on the line);
    H in the left slot and Y, a tight end split out, in the right slot, both a step off the ball."""
    return line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, rb_w, "R"),
                      O("X", "WR", LINE_D, x_w), O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, h_w),
                      O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, y_w), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, z_w)]


def cover3(nb_side=1, cb_d=7.0, cb_out=1.0, x_w=-15.0, z_w=15.0, extra=None):
    """A 4-2-5 nickel showing Cover 3 against 2x2: corners off with outside leverage, one deep
    safety, and a curl-flat defender walked down over each slot: the nickel ($) on side
    `nb_side` (+1 = offense's right) and the strong safety on the other. extra = {key: (d, w)}."""
    s = nb_side
    out = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.4, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"),
           D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"), D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E"),
           D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W"),
           D("LCB", "CB", cb_d, x_w - cb_out, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", cb_d, z_w + cb_out, "CB"),
           D("NB", "NB", 5.0, s * 7.2, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 5.5, -s * 7.2, "SS"),
           D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0, "FS")]
    extra = extra or {}
    return [q.moved(d=extra[q.key][0], w=extra[q.key][1]) if q.key in extra else q for q in out]


def protect(p, rushers=("WDE", "WDT", "SDT", "SDE"), depth=1.2, rush=1.6):
    """Linemen set, four rushers engage them: enough to say 'pass', no more."""
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-depth, 0.0)])
    for k in rushers:
        if k in p.players:
            p.rush(k, pts=[(-rush, 0.0)], speed=2.0)


def go_to(p, key, end, kind="path", delay=0.0, speed=None, via=()):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end`."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "rush":
        return p.rush(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "route":
        return p.route(key, pts, frame="field", delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run}[kind](key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- drawing helpers
def _P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def clean(ax):
    """Drop the painted yard numbers (they sit where receivers stand); clip all text to the window."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def ruler(fld, p, fs=6.0, step=5, top=30):
    """Depth labels (yards past the line of scrimmage) just inside the left edge of the window."""
    xl = (160 / 3) - fld.y1 + 0.4
    for d in range(step, top + 1, step):
        y = p.los + d
        if fld.x0 + 1.5 <= y <= fld.x1 - 1.5:
            fld.ax.text(xl, y, f"{d}" + (" yd" if d == step else ""), fontsize=fs, color=style.INK_2,
                        ha="left", va="center", zorder=12,
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))


def draw(p, width_in=6.2, ax=None, show_ruler=True, **kw):
    fld = p.draw(width_in=width_in, ax=ax, title=False, **kw)
    clean(fld.ax)
    if show_ruler:
        ruler(fld, p)
    return fld


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.2, ha="center", weight="normal", box=True):
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=13,
                fontweight=weight, linespacing=1.15,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9) if box else None)


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7, ha="center"):
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = _P(fld, p, *text_at), _P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=13, linespacing=1.15,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=7),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def branch(fld, p, pts, color=READ_GREEN, lw=1.7, dash=(0, (3, 2.2)), end="arrow"):
    """A dashed path through absolute (d, w) points: the other branch of a read, or a defender's reaction."""
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=5, solid_capstyle="round")
    if end == "arrow":
        fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=10, color=color, lw=lw, zorder=5))


def taken(fld, p, pts, lw=1.4):
    """A route the defender has taken away: grey, dashed, with an X at the end."""
    branch(fld, p, pts, color=GREY, lw=lw, dash=(0, (2, 2)), end="none")
    x, y = _P(fld, p, *pts[-1])
    fld.ax.plot([float(x)], [float(y)], marker="X", ms=8, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, mec="white", mew=0.7, zorder=9)


def opening(fld, p, center, size, color=style.THIRD):
    """A soft green oval: the throwing window that opens."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, *center)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), size[1], size[0], fc=color, alpha=0.2, ec=color, lw=1.0,
                             zorder=1.6))


def triangle(fld, p, pts, color=style.THIRD):
    xy = [tuple(float(v) for v in _P(fld, p, *q)) for q in pts]
    fld.ax.add_patch(Polygon(xy, closed=True, fc=color, alpha=0.15, ec=color, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=1.7))


def bracket(fld, p, d, w0, w1, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7, dy=1.2):
    """A horizontal dimension line at depth d from w0 to w1, labelled above."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d, w0), _P(fld, p, d, w1)
    fld.ax.annotate("", (float(x1), float(y1)), xytext=(float(x0), float(y0)),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=color, lw=0.8), zorder=6)
    say(fld, p, d + dy, (w0 + w1) / 2, text, color=color, fontsize=fontsize)


def vbracket(fld, p, w, d0, d1, color=style.INK_2):
    """A vertical dimension line at width w from depth d0 to d1."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d0, w), _P(fld, p, d1, w)
    fld.ax.annotate("", (float(x1), float(y1)), xytext=(float(x0), float(y0)),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=color, lw=0.8), zorder=6)


def panel_title(ax, text, fs=9):
    ax.set_title(text, fontsize=fs, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")


LEGEND = {
    "route": Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.8, label="route"),
    "block": Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.8, marker="|", ms=8, mew=2.2, label="block"),
    "run": Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=2.6, label="ball carrier"),
    "pass": Line2D([], [], color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 2)), label="the throw"),
    "drop": Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), label="defender's drop"),
    "react": Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (3, 2.2)), label="defender's reaction"),
    "other": Line2D([], [], color=READ_GREEN, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (3, 2.2)), label="the other branch"),
    "read": Line2D([], [], color=style.THIRD, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (4, 2)), label="QB's read"),
    "window": Patch(fc=style.THIRD, alpha=0.25, ec=style.THIRD, label="window that opens"),
    "triangle": Patch(fc=style.THIRD, alpha=0.15, ec=style.THIRD, ls=(0, (4, 2)), label="the triangle"),
    "zone": Patch(fc=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.13, ec=style.DEFENSE, ls=(0, (3, 2)), label="zone defender's area"),
    "taken": Line2D([], [], color=GREY, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 2)), marker="X", ms=7, mfc=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
                    mec="white", label="taken away"),
}


def legend(fig, keys, ncol=None, y=0.0, fs=7):
    hs = [LEGEND[k] for k in keys]
    fig.legend(handles=hs, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, y), ncol=ncol or len(hs), fontsize=fs,
               frameon=False, handlelength=2.0, columnspacing=1.0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- frame strips (print) and video (web)
MARK_R = 0.7


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def frame_panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window_, rings=(), throw_t=None):
    """One moment of a simulated play, with faint trails, optional rings and the ball's flight so far."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window_, numbers=False, hashes=True,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    shown = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window_[0] + 0.4, play.los + window_[1] - 0.4)
                & cur["y"].between(ylo + 0.4, yhi - 0.4)]
    ids = set(shown["_id"])
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(ids) & (df["side"] != "ball")]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.45, zorder=3)
    if throw_t is not None and t > throw_t:
        b = df[(df["side"] == "ball") & (df["frameId"] <= fid)]
        b = b[b["time"] >= throw_t - 0.05]
        xs, ys = fld.xy(b["x"].values, b["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=9)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for _, rr in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(rr["x"], rr["y"]))
        if rr["side"] == "ball":
            if throw_t is None or t <= throw_t:
                # still in the quarterback's hands: draw it at his throwing shoulder so his letter stays readable
                x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(rr["x"], rr["y"] - 1.0))
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y), 0.9, 0.56, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=11))
            continue
        lab = str(rr.get("label", "") or "")
        if rr["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), MARK_R, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARK_R * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(8.0, ppy * (0.85 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.62)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in rings:
        rr = cur[cur["displayName"] == key].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(rr["x"], rr["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), MARK_R * 1.6, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.7, zorder=7))
    return fld


def strip(play, times, notes=None, lateral=(-24, 4), window=(-8, 14), ncols=2, rings=(), throw_t=None,
          width_in=6.5):
    df = tracking(play)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]), window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + (0.6 if notes else 0.25))))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
        frame_panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, throw_t)
        lab = "snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  {lab}", fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        if notes:
            ax.text(0.5, -0.03, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7.3,
                    color=style.INK, linespacing=1.2)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=2.2 if notes else 0.6, w_pad=0.6)
    return fig


def video(play, times, notes=None, lateral=(-24, 4), window=(-8, 14), rings=(), throw_t=None, width_in=5.6):
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    df = tracking(play)
    span_w, span_d = abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]), window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.4))
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()

    def update(fid):
        ax.clear()
        t = float(tmap[fid])
        frame_panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, throw_t)
        txt = "snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
        if notes:
            cur = [n for tt, n in zip(times, notes) if tt <= t + 1e-6]
            txt += ("   " + cur[-1].replace("\n", " ")) if cur else ""
        ax.set_title(txt, fontsize=8, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=sorted(df["frameId"].unique()), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def play_movie(play, times, notes=None, **kw):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if PDF:
        strip(play, times, notes=notes, **kw)
        plt.show()
    else:
        kw.pop("ncols", None)
        kw.pop("width_in", None)
        video(play, times, notes=notes, **kw)


def trail(p, key, target, jab, lag=0.35, off=(-1.1, -0.9), t_open=0.35, t_on=0.9, t_end=4.0):
    """Hand-made keyframes for a defender chasing `target` from behind: he steps to `jab` (a
    reaction to the release), then settles `off` = (down, toward the offense's right) yards from
    where the receiver was `lag` seconds earlier. (gridiron's man() ends on top of the receiver.)
    His depth is floored so he never ends up in the offense's backfield: while the receiver is near the
    line the defender stays hip to hip with him, then the floor relaxes and he trails a step behind."""
    kf, t0, t1 = p._compile()
    kf = dict(kf)
    q = p.players[key]
    rows = [(min(t0, -1.0), q.d, q.w), (0.0, q.d, q.w), (t_open, *jab)]
    for tt in np.round(np.arange(t_open + 0.05, t_end, 0.05), 3):
        f = min(1.0, (tt - t_open) / (t_on - t_open))
        f = f * f * (3 - 2 * f)
        chase = p.position(target, max(0.0, tt - lag)) + np.array(off)
        now_d = float(p.position(target, tt)[0])
        chase[0] = max(chase[0], 0.3, now_d - 0.6 - 0.5 * max(0.0, now_d - 1.5))
        rows.append((tt, *(np.array(jab) * (1 - f) + chase * f)))
    kf[key] = np.array(rows)
    p._compiled = (kf, t0, max(t1, t_end))


def catch_time(p):
    """Seconds after the snap at which the first pass arrives (rounded up to a tenth)."""
    for kind, to, te in p.ball_events:
        if kind == "pass":
            a, b = p.pass_target_spot()
            return float(np.ceil((te + np.hypot(*(b - a)) / gp.BALL_SPEED) * 10) / 10)
``````

``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (2025 dropbacks with time to throw, from nflverse)"}
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp


def dropbacks(season=2025):
    """Regular-season dropbacks (spikes removed) with nflverse participation (time to throw, pressure,
    rushers; FTN-sourced from 2023) joined on."""
    cols = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "pass_attempt", "sack", "qb_scramble", "qb_spike",
            "qb_dropback", "complete_pass", "air_yards", "yards_after_catch", "receiving_yards", "epa", "success"]
    plays = pbp([season], columns=cols)
    plays = plays[(plays["season_type"] == "REG") & (plays["qb_dropback"] == 1) & (plays["qb_spike"] != 1)]
    part = nfl().load_participation([season]).to_pandas().rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id"})
    part = part[["game_id", "play_id", "time_to_throw", "was_pressure", "number_of_pass_rushers"]]
    return plays.merge(part, on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="left")
```

## What the quick game is

The [**quick game**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-quick-game) is the set of pass plays
built to get the ball out in roughly **2.5 seconds or less**. Three things make a pass play
"quick," and they go together:

1. **A short drop.** From under center, the quarterback takes three steps back (a
   [three-step drop](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)); from the shotgun, already five yards
   deep, he takes one step (some teams teach three quick, short steps that cover the same
   ground). There's no time to drift, reset or scan.
2. **Short routes.** Most receivers break at five or six yards or less: slants, hitches,
   flats, short outs. One receiver often runs deep, but mainly to drag a defender out of the
   way.
3. **A throw timed to the break.** The ball leaves as the quarterback's back foot lands,
   aimed at the spot where the receiver *will be* when he makes his cut. If the throw is
   late, the play is usually dead.

Nothing in the rulebook defines it, and teams draw the line in different places, but
analysts usually treat throws out in under 2.5 seconds as "quick." In 2025 about half of
all NFL pass attempts came out that fast; the median attempt left the quarterback's hand at
2.5 seconds.[^ttt25] That's the first thing to understand about the quick game: it is not a
gadget or a change-up. It is a large share of everything an NFL offense throws.

## Why it exists: three jobs

The quick game survives in every playbook, from the old 49ers to the modern Chiefs,
because it does three jobs no other part of the offense does as cheaply.

**Job 1: beat the pass rush with the clock.** A pass rush is a race. Four rushers against
five blockers usually need well over two and a half seconds to get home, if they get there at
all; a blitzer nobody blocks can arrive in about two. The quarterback can win that race in
two ways: block long enough for the deep routes to develop, or throw before the rush
matters. The quick game is the second way. It can't be sacked if the ball is already gone,
and it doesn't need the offensive line to win, only to hold for a heartbeat. The linemen block
it differently, too. A quick throw is released low and early, from a quarterback only a step or
two behind them, so they meet the rushers aggressively at the line (the
[jump set](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-jump-set) of [Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd))
to keep the defenders' hands down and out of the throwing lanes. A defensive lineman who gets
his arms up in the gap the slant is thrown through is the quick game's most common way to lose
a ball: the batted pass.

[Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd) showed one half of the clock's bargain: the longer
the ball stays in the quarterback's hand, the more often the rush gets to him (under one throw
in ten is pressured when it comes out in under two seconds; about half when it is held three
and a half seconds or more). Here is the other half, the price of throwing early.

Fast and short come as a package: the quick throws went only three to seven yards past the
line of scrimmage on average, against eleven or twelve for the slow ones.

**Job 2: keep the offense on schedule.** A [first down](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)
takes ten yards in three plays, and the plays that kill drives are the ones that lose yards
or gain none: sacks, incompletions, and the third-and-long that follows them. Coaches call
staying ahead of the chains being
[on schedule](../10-situational-football/10-01-early-downs-and-field-zones.qmd): roughly,
gaining four or more on first down and half the remaining distance on second. Quick throws
are completed far more often (in 2025, about 72% of attempts out in under 2.5 seconds were
caught, against 57% of the rest) and almost never end in a sack, so they keep the offense
in second-and-5 instead of second-and-10.[^ttt25b] By
[success rate](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd) (the share of
plays with positive EPA, meaning plays that left the offense better off than before the snap),
quick throws succeeded on about 51% of attempts, slower throws on about 45%.

**Job 3: stretch the run game sideways.** Bill Walsh, who built the most influential short
passing offense in NFL history, started from a team that couldn't run the ball well enough to
control a game, so he used short, high-percentage throws to do the running game's job; his
throws have often been described as extended handoffs.[^walshrun] A five-yard pass to a
receiver near the sideline gets the ball to a fast player in space, away from the big
defenders in the middle, and lets him run. In 2025 about 59% of the receiving yards on
quick completions came *after* the catch, against about 38% on slower ones.[^yac] That is
the defining fact of the quick game: the throw is short and the run after it does most of the
work. It also means that a defense that wants to stop the quick game has to tackle in space,
on the edges of the field, where it has the fewest defenders.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists, and what it costs"}
The quick game trades **depth for certainty**: a high chance of a small gain, a near-zero
chance of a sack and a receiver running before the defense is set, in place of the big gain
through the air. The bill comes in three parts. First, **the defense can squeeze it.** If an offense never
threatens deep, defenders creep closer and the short windows shrink; quick game works best
when the defense still has to respect the deep ball. Second, **it needs yards after the
catch**: a five-yard throw that is tackled at five yards on third-and-7 is a punt. Third, **it
gets harder as the field shrinks**: near the goal line there is less room to run after the
catch. The rest of this chapter is about how good offenses keep the bargain on their side.
:::

### A short history: the rest of the Walsh story

You met the start of this story in [Passing Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd): Bill
Walsh, an assistant on Paul Brown's Cincinnati Bengals in 1970, building a passing game of short,
timed throws around Virgil Carter, a quarterback who was accurate but had no deep arm, and Carter
leading the NFL in completion percentage in 1971.[^carter] Two details sharpen it. Carter was
never supposed to be the starter: the Bengals' brilliant young quarterback, Greg Cook, had wrecked
his throwing shoulder as a rookie in 1969, so Walsh built the offense around the quarterback he
had, not the one he wanted. And Carter, who had studied statistics in college and took an MBA
during his playing career, co-wrote one of the first academic papers to estimate the
[expected points](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd)
value of field position: the same idea this book uses as its scorecard.[^machol]

In San Francisco from 1979, with Joe Montana, the approach became the backbone of three Super
Bowl champions (after the 1981, 1984 and 1988 seasons).[^walsh] Its signature was the slant to
Jerry Rice, thrown on rhythm before the cornerback could react and turned into a long touchdown
by Rice's speed: Rice caught a record 22 touchdown passes in just 12 games in 1987.[^rice] The
family of offenses descended from Walsh's ideas came to be called the West Coast offense, a label
with a tangled history that [Offensive Systems and Languages](04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd)
untangles.

A rule change helped. In 1978 the NFL barred defenders from contacting receivers more than
five yards past the line of scrimmage; until then a defensive back could keep bumping a
receiver well down the field.[^blount] Receivers who could no longer be mugged at
eight and ten yards made short timing routes far more reliable, and passing numbers rose
across the league. Walsh arrived in San Francisco a year later.

## Rhythm: the drop and the throw are one motion

Watch a quick throw from the end-zone camera and you'll notice that the quarterback never
seems to *decide* anything. He catches the snap, takes his steps, and the ball is gone on
the last one. That is a [**rhythm throw**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rhythm-throw): a
pass thrown on the last step of the drop, with no hitch or hesitation, so the ball arrives
just as the receiver breaks.

The rhythm is the whole point. The quarterback's drop and the receiver's route are
designed together, step for step: a three-step drop under center, or a one-step drop from the
shotgun, is timed to a receiver who breaks at about five or six yards
([Passing Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd) lays out the matched pairs). When the
quarterback's back foot hits, the receiver is making his cut, and the ball leaves. If the
quarterback has to hitch (take an extra reset step) or look somewhere else, the timing is gone
and a different, slower play has begun.

You'll meet three different clocks in this chapter, and they measure different things:

- **About 1 to 1.5 seconds** is the *design*: from the shotgun, a rhythm throw against a
  receiver who gets a clean release leaves the hand about then.
- **2.5 seconds** is the *analysts' line*, the cut-off the data in this chapter uses to call a
  throw "quick." It sits well past the design time because real plays lose a beat here and
  there: a receiver delayed by a jam, a quarterback who waits half a second for a defender to
  commit, a snap that comes late in his hands. A 2.1-second slant against press is still a
  quick-game throw; it just shows you the press cost the receiver a step.
- **"One-thousand-two"** is the *couch rule* in the "Watch for it" box at the end: if the ball
  is gone before you finish saying it, you saw the quick game working as designed.

What does a *late* quick throw look like? The quarterback's last step lands and the ball
doesn't come out: he hitches, or his shoulders turn to another receiver, and the slant runner is
already two or three steps past his break, drifting into the linebackers. When the throw finally
comes, the defender who was a step behind is now at the catch point. That is when you see the
batted balls, the contested catches and the interceptions on short routes.

That has a consequence that shapes the whole quick game: **the quarterback has almost no
time to read the defense after the snap.** He gets one look, at one defender, and has to
know in advance what that defender's answer means. Most of the "reading" therefore happens
*before* the snap. To see how, we need one more piece of vocabulary.

## Leverage: the pre-snap read

Look at any cornerback before the snap and ask a simple question: is he lined up *inside*
the receiver, *outside* him, or straight in front of him? That position is his
[**leverage**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-leverage-inside-outside), and it is the most
important thing a quarterback looks at before a quick throw.

Why would a defender give anything away on purpose? Because he can't take everything
away, so he takes away what his teammates can't help him with. A defender usually lines up on
the side **where he has no help**, and funnels the receiver toward the side where he does.
A cornerback with a safety deep in the middle and linebackers underneath often plays outside
leverage: his teammates can help on routes inside. A corner whose help is outside plays inside
leverage, and that help can be a teammate sitting in the flat in front of him or simply the
sideline. Coaches call the sideline the cornerback's twelfth man, because a receiver near it has
nowhere to go but inside or straight up. So leverage is not just one man's position. It is a
clue to the whole coverage behind him.

The receiver's [split](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-split-receiver-split), how far from the
ball he lines up, feeds the same read from the other side. Split wide, near the sideline, he has
little room to break outside, so the corner can shade him inside and let the sideline do the
rest. A receiver who *reduces* his split, lining up closer to the ball, has room both ways, and
a defender who sees a reduced split starts expecting an outside-breaking route.

The quarterback's rule is short: **throw away from leverage.** A route that breaks toward the
side the defender *isn't* on gains a step at the break, because the defender has to cross the
receiver's path, or run around him, to get there. That's the core of the
[**pre-snap read**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pre-snap-read): a look at the defense's
alignment before the snap (leverage, the
[cushion](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd), meaning how far off the
receiver the defender stands, the safeties, the box) that tells the quarterback which side, or
which receiver, a play should go to. Many quick-game calls are drawn with a concept on *each*
side of the formation for exactly this reason: the quarterback picks the side whose leverage
he likes before the ball is snapped, then reads one defender on that side after it. The
coordinator calls the play; the quarterback chooses the side, at the line, inside the rules the
offense has practiced all week (many teams pre-set a default, such as "work the side with the
extra receiver," for when both look equal).

Three numbers belong in every pre-snap read of a single receiver:

- **Inside, outside or [head-up](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-head-up)?** Head-up
  (straight in front of the receiver) is a defender who hasn't given a side away. It is
  common in press coverage, and the release section below shows how a receiver deals with it.
- **How deep?** A defender seven or eight yards off can't stop a short throw from being
  caught; he can only tackle the catch. One pressed up at the line (in
  [press](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd) coverage: a yard or so away,
  ready to jam the receiver at the snap) can disrupt the route itself.
- **Where is his help?** A deep safety over the top lets a cornerback sit on short routes.
  No safety at all means the cornerback has to protect against the deep ball first.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The quarterback reads the coverage after the snap." For deep dropback passes, mostly yes.
For the quick game, the important decision is made before the snap and the post-snap read is
a single glance at a single defender. When you see a quarterback throw the instant his foot
lands, he isn't guessing; he made the decision ten seconds earlier, from the alignment, and
the snap merely confirmed it.
:::

## Slant-flat: the high-low

Now the concepts. A [pass concept](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd) is a set of routes designed
to work together, usually to put one defender in a position where he can't be right. Every
quick concept in this chapter is built on one of the two stretches from
[Passing Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd): a
[high-low](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-high-low-read) (one receiver above a defender, one
below him) or a [horizontal stretch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-horizontal-stretch) (one
inside him, one outside him). The
defender being stretched is the one the quarterback watches.

The simplest quick concept in football is
[**slant-flat**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slant-flat). The outside receiver runs a
slant: three hard steps upfield, then a sharp break inside at about 45 degrees. The inside
receiver runs to the flat, the area near the sideline just past the line of scrimmage. Between
them stands one defender, usually the slot defender or an outside linebacker, whose job in
most zone coverages is to guard the short area outside: the *flat defender* (or, in Cover 3
language, the
[curl-flat defender](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd)). He is the read.

The quarterback's thought process is one sentence long: **"If the flat defender widens,
throw the slant; if he sits, throw the flat."** He doesn't have to diagnose the coverage, find
the safeties or work through five receivers. He has to watch one man take one step. That's
why slant-flat is often the first pass concept a young quarterback learns, and why it
survives at every level of the sport.

Notice what each route is doing to the defender. The flat route is a *low* threat: it pulls
him toward the sideline and forward. The slant is a *high* threat: it attacks the space
behind him and inside him. It is the same high-low as the curl-flat read in
[Passing Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd), squeezed into three steps. He can't be
in both places, and he has to commit in about half a second. If he widens, he has opened the
door the slant runs through. If he stays put, or sinks into the slant's path, the inside
receiver catches the ball in the flat with no one within five yards, which on most downs is a
fine result: a "long handoff" to the edge.

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: what the read defender can do"}
Coaches describe the one defender's choice with a handful of verbs. You'll see them through
the rest of this chapter:

| He... | What he does | Throw to |
|---|---|---|
| **widens** | runs toward the sideline with the outside or flat route | the route inside him or behind him |
| **sits** | holds his spot | the route he isn't standing on |
| **sinks** | drops deeper, under the higher route (coaches say he *robs* it) | the low route in front of him |
| **jumps** (or **drives**) | runs forward at the short route | the route behind him |
| **carries** | runs up the field with a vertical route | the short route he left |
| **bails** | turns and runs deep at the snap (as Cover 3 cornerbacks do) | the short route in front of him |

A defense that wants to take slant-flat away coaches its flat defender to *sink* under the
slant and trusts a cornerback squatting in the flat to take the other route, which is why
slant-flat struggles against [Cover 2](../06-pass-coverage/06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd).
:::

::: {#cell-fig-slant-flat .cell execution_count=5}

What does slant-flat give up? Depth. The best case is a slant caught at seven or eight
yards with room to run; the usual case is a flat route for four or five. It also needs the
cornerback to cooperate: against a corner who sits low in the flat (as in
[Cover 2](../06-pass-coverage/06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd), where corners squat short), the
flat is covered by a second man and the slant must fit into a tighter window. That's where
the other concepts come in.

## Stick: the in-out

[**Stick**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stick) is one of the most-called quick concepts in
the NFL, and you met it in [What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)
as that chapter's one example play. Here is why it is so popular. Slant-flat stretches the
flat defender vertically; stick stretches him *horizontally*, inside and outside, at a depth
that usually reaches the line to gain on second or third and medium.

Three receivers on one side. The outside man (#1) runs off, deep: a go route or a fade that
carries the cornerback away. One man runs to about six yards, at or just past the line to gain,
and **sticks**: he settles in the open space and turns to face the quarterback, or, against man
coverage, breaks away from his defender. One man runs to the flat, getting to the numbers or
wider. The stick sits inside the flat defender; the flat route goes outside him.

Which man runs which route depends on the formation, and you'll see both versions on Sundays.
In the trips version you met in [What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)
(sometimes called *Y-stick*), the tight end is #3, the innermost receiver, and runs the stick,
while #2 runs an arrow to the flat outside him. In the 2x2 version drawn below, the classic NFL
drawing, the tight end is #2 and runs the stick, and the running back comes out of the backfield
to the flat. The rule underneath is the same: the stick runner settles inside the flat defender,
and the flat comes from whoever is outside or under him.

::: {#cell-fig-stick .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def stick_play(nb_widens):
    off = spread(rb_w=1.5)
    dfn = cover3(nb_side=1)
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=6)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(2.0)
    p.route("Z", r.go(16.0))
    p.route("Y", r.stick(7.5))
    p.route("RB", r.path((0.5, 4.5), (1.4, 8.5), (5.2, 11.8), (6.8, 13.6)), side=1)
    p.drop("RCB", (13.5, 17.5))
    p.drop("MIKE", (7.2, 2.6), delay=0.15)
    p.highlight("NB")
    p.pass_to("Y" if nb_widens else "RB", t=1.4)
    return p


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.05))
for ax, widen in zip(axes, (True, False)):
    p = stick_play(widen)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-11.5, 25.5), window=(-8.5, 15.5), show_ruler=False)
    if widen:
        branch(fld, p, [(5.0, 7.2), (3.6, 11.0), (3.0, 13.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
        opening(fld, p, (5.9, 8.4), (3.4, 4.8))
        say(fld, p, 11.0, 7.0, "stick: open in\nthe space he left", color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, 3.8, 21.4, "$ widens", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        panel_title(ax, "$ widens: throw the stick")
    else:
        branch(fld, p, [(5.0, 7.2), (6.0, 8.2)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
        opening(fld, p, (1.8, 14.4), (3.0, 4.6))
        say(fld, p, 11.0, 7.0, "$ sits inside,\nunder the stick", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        say(fld, p, -3.2, 16.0, "flat: open", color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
        panel_title(ax, "$ sits: throw the flat")
legend(fig, ["route", "react", "pass", "window"], y=0.09)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8, rect=(0, 0.08, 1, 1))
plt.show()
```

The ringed nickel back ($) is the read, and the two panels are his two choices. Left: he widens toward the back in the flat, so the stick is open in the space he left. Right: he sits, staying inside under the stick, so the back is alone in the flat at the numbers. The Mike linebacker (M) drops to the middle and is too far inside to help on the stick in time; the cornerback goes deep with Z.](04-03-quick-game_files/figure-html/fig-stick-output-1.svg){#fig-stick}

The stick route itself is the clever part. It isn't a hitch with a fixed landmark; it's a rule.
Against zone, the receiver finds the soft spot between the flat defender and the next defender
inside (the Mike linebacker here) and sits in it, facing the quarterback, so the ball can be
thrown the moment he settles. Against man coverage, there is no soft spot to find, because a
defender is following him, so he breaks away from that defender's leverage, in or out. That's
an [option route](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd) in miniature, and it is why the quarterback
and the stick runner rehearse it endlessly: both of them have to see the same thing.

Stick is everywhere because it does three things at once: it puts the ball at or near the line
to gain on the downs where five or six yards matter most; it works against nearly every zone,
because nearly all of them have *one* defender responsible for both the area inside and the area
outside at that depth; and the clear-out by #1 keeps a deep threat on the field, so the cornerback
can't come up and sit on everything short.

## Snag: the triangle

Slant-flat stretches one defender up and down; stick stretches him side to side.
[**Snag**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-snag) does both at once by putting three
receivers in a triangle, so two defenders are stuck guarding three spots. (Some teams call
it *spot*.)

::: {#cell-fig-snag .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = spread(rb_w=1.5)
dfn = cover3(nb_side=1)
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.0)
p.route("Z", r.path((4.0, 0.0), (5.5, -1.5), (5.2, -3.5)))
p.route("Y", r.path((5.5, 0.0), (8.5, 0.0), (14.0, 6.5)))
p.route("RB", r.path((0.5, 5.5), (2.0, 10.0), (2.7, 13.5), (6.0, 16.5)), side=1)
p.drop("RCB", (12.5, 17.5))
p.drop("MIKE", (7.0, 3.0), delay=0.15)
p.highlight("NB")
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-19.0, 26.0), window=(-8.5, 20.5), show_ruler=False)
triangle(fld, p, [(12.5, 15.5), (4.5, 11.5), (1.0, 18.0)])
say(fld, p, 13.4, 13.0, "corner (high)", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
point_to(fld, p, (2.2, 9.6), (4.6, 11.5), "snag", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -0.6, 21.2, "flat (low)", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 16.0, -10.2, "The reads\n"
    "vs Cover 3 (this look), watch the $:\n"
    "   $ widens?  Snag, inside him.\n"
    "   $ sits on the snag?  Flat.\n"
    "vs Cover 2, watch the cornerback:\n"
    "   CB squats in the flat?  Corner.",
    color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=6.8, ha="center")
legend(fld.fig, ["route", "drop", "triangle"], y=0.07)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Snag to the offense's right against a Cover 3 look. Z, the outside receiver, pushes upfield five yards and settles just inside where he started (the snag). Y, from the slot, runs a corner route over the top, toward the sideline about fifteen yards deep. The running back runs to the flat. Together they make a triangle (shaded): a high-low on the cornerback (corner route over, flat under) and an in-out on the flat defender (snag inside, flat outside). The receivers on the other side are left out. The quarterback's reads are in the box: against this look, the $.](04-03-quick-game_files/figure-html/fig-snag-output-1.svg){#fig-snag}
:::
:::


Snag is read against the coverage the quarterback identified before the snap. Against
**Cover 3**, the look drawn here, the cornerback has a deep third and bails, so the corner route
is covered before it starts. The quarterback's eyes go straight to the flat defender, the $,
exactly as in stick: if he widens to the flat, throw the snag inside him; if he sits on the snag,
throw the flat. Against [Cover 2](../06-pass-coverage/06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd), the
cornerback squats in the flat with a safety deep behind him, and the read moves to the top of
the triangle: if the corner squats on the flat route, the corner route goes over his head into the
hole in front of the safety; if he sinks under the corner route, the flat is open.

So why call snag instead of stick? Against Cover 3 they are close cousins that read the same
man. Snag's extra is the corner route. Stick's flat route runs straight into a Cover 2
cornerback squatting in the flat; snag throws over him. A quarterback who isn't sure before the
snap whether he will see Cover 3 or Cover 2 has an answer to both in one call.

Because the triangle combines both kinds of stretch, a single adjustment can't take it away; the
[triangle read](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd) becomes a whole family in the next chapter, with
deeper routes and more time.

## Spacing: five windows

Every concept so far stretches one or two defenders. [**Spacing**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spacing)
stretches the whole underneath coverage: four or five receivers settle at about the same depth,
five or six yards, at even intervals across the field, each in the gap between two zone
defenders. You saw the geometry in [Passing Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)'s
horizontal stretch (five receivers against Cover 3's four underneath defenders). As a called
concept it adds two things.

First, **one route goes underneath.** Almost every spacing call sends one receiver, often the
back or the innermost slot, on an arrow or flat route to the sideline at two or three yards. Without
it, the curl-flat defender can sit at five yards on the hitch and nobody punishes him; with it,
he is in a high-low as well. Second, **the quarterback works one half of the field.** He can't
watch five receivers in a second and a half, so before the snap he picks a side, usually the
one where the offense has more receivers than the defense has underneath defenders, and after it
he reads one man on that side.

::: {#cell-fig-spacing .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = spread(rb_w=1.5)
dfn = cover3(nb_side=1, extra={"SS": (7.5, -11.5), "WILL": (7.5, -4.0), "MIKE": (7.5, 3.5), "NB": (7.0, 11.0),
                                 "LCB": (11.5, -17.5), "RCB": (11.5, 17.5), "FS": (14.5, 0.0)})
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.0)
p.route("X", r.hitch(6.2))
p.route("Z", r.hitch(6.2))
p.route("H", r.path((6.5, 0.0), (7.0, -1.2)))     # settles inside, in the gap between the SS and the W
p.route("Y", r.path((6.5, 0.0), (7.0, -1.8)))     # settles inside, between the M and the $
go_to(p, "RB", (2.4, 15.5), kind="route", via=[(-3.6, 4.0), (0.2, 9.5)])
for k in ("SS", "WILL", "MIKE", "NB"):
    q = p.players[k]
    p.zone((q.d, q.w), (3.5, 6.0))
p.highlight("NB")
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-25.0, 25.0), window=(-8.5, 19.0))
for k in ("X", "H", "Y", "Z"):
    opening(fld, p, tuple(p._cur(k)), (2.4, 2.8))
opening(fld, p, (2.4, 15.5), (2.4, 2.8))
branch(fld, p, [(7.0, 11.0), (5.2, 14.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
branch(fld, p, [(7.0, 11.0), (7.4, 8.6)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
say(fld, p, 14.6, 9.6, "$ widens to the flat?\nthrow Z's hitch or Y.\n$ sits on Z? the flat.",
    color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, -5.4, 13.0, "his side: 3 receivers\nvs 2 defenders", color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -5.4, -13.0, "the other side: 2 vs 2", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7)
legend(fld.fig, ["route", "zone", "react", "window"], y=0.07)
```

Spacing is the quick game's answer to a defense that plays zone and refuses to rush more than
four. Its weakness is the mirror image: against man coverage there are no gaps to sit in, so
the receivers have to beat their men, and the sitting routes turn into breaks away from
leverage, the same rule as the stick route.

Spacing is an old idea, and a natural fit for the Air Raid offenses of Hal Mumme and Mike Leach
in college football, which spread receivers across the whole width of the field and made the
quick game one of their foundations;[^airraid]
[The College Laboratory](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd) tells that story.

## Speed out: beating a soft corner to the sideline

Not every quick throw is a two-man read. The
[**speed out**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-speed-out) is a single receiver's route,
thrown on timing against one particular look: a cornerback playing well off, with inside
leverage, who is backing up at the snap. (Names vary by system: some playbooks call this
five-yard rounded cut the *quick out* and save "speed out" for a deeper rounded out off a longer
drop. The route here is the short one.)

::: {#cell-fig-speed-out .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = spread()
dfn = cover3(nb_side=1, cb_d=8.0, cb_out=-1.0,
             extra={"SS": (12.0, -9.0), "FS": (12.0, 11.8), "NB": (5.0, 6.8), "MIKE": (4.5, 1.8)})
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(1.5)
p.route("Z", [(0, 0), (3.0, 0.0), (4.1, 0.25), (4.8, 0.9), (5.15, 1.8), (5.2, 2.9), (5.0, 4.6), (4.7, 7.0)],
        speed=7.5)                                   # a rounded break: the turn is spread over several steps
p.route("Y", r.seam(14.0))
p.drop("RCB", (11.0, 14.6), delay=0.1)
p.drop("FS", (14.8, 12.6))
p.pass_to("Z", t=0.8)
p.highlight("RCB")
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-6.5, 25.5), window=(-8.5, 17.5))
vbracket(fld, p, 12.0, -0.7, 8.0)
say(fld, p, 5.4, 12.5, "8-yard\ncushion", fontsize=7, ha="left")
point_to(fld, p, (13.0, 19.6), (8.0, 14.0), "CB inside Z\n(inside leverage),\nbacking up", fontsize=7)
point_to(fld, p, (1.2, 22.4), (4.1, 15.9), "rounded\nbreak", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -6.4, 11.5, "ball out as the drop\nlands, before the break", color=style.BALL, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 15.2, 6.0, "seam holds\nthe safety", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

Z runs four or five hard steps and rounds his break toward the sideline without slowing down (the curve, not a square corner); the quarterback throws as his one-step drop lands (from under center, on his third step), before Z has even turned, aiming at the sideline. Y's seam route keeps the safety on that side deep and out of the throw. The pass travels farther than any other quick throw, so it needs an accurate, strong arm.](04-03-quick-game_files/figure-html/fig-speed-out-output-1.svg){#fig-speed-out}

Why would a cornerback line up inside in the first place? The leverage rule answers it: he
lines up where he has no help. Against a two-high look nobody sits in the deep middle, so the
routes that hurt him are the post and the dig, breaking inside toward all that open grass, while
the sideline protects his outside. (In a quarters-style coverage there's a second reason: the
safety on that side is reading the slot, so the corner is effectively alone on Z, backing up to
stay on top of him.)

Why does the speed out beat that? Because the cornerback's alignment has already made a promise.
Lined up inside and eight yards off, he is protecting the middle of the field and the deep ball,
and the sideline in front of him is the one area he has conceded. A receiver who runs at him
hard and rounds his break toward the sideline, without the throttle-down of a square cut,
gets there first. The ball has to beat the corner's break, which is why the speed out is a
[timing route](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd): the quarterback lets it go before the receiver turns, to a spot, and trusts
him to be there.

It is also the quick throw that most exposes a quarterback's arm. The ball travels from the
middle of the field to the sideline, the longest flight in the quick game, and a throw that
floats lets a defender close on it. The dangerous defender is usually not the corner on top but
one underneath: a [Cover 2](../06-pass-coverage/06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd) cornerback
squatting in the flat, or a Cover 3 curl-flat defender who sinks and widens under the out (the $
in the figure, if he reads it). An interception there has an open field in front of it, which is
why coaches call the out a risky throw for a weak arm and why the speed out is a pre-snap call
against one look, not a throw into any coverage.

## Two more pairs: double slants and hitch-seam

Two last concepts round out the core of the quick game. Each pairs two receivers on one side.

[**Double slants**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-double-slants): both receivers run
slants, one shallower and quicker, the other a step deeper, so their paths stack one above the
other as they cross in front of the linebackers. (Teams differ on which one goes underneath;
many NFL playbooks have the inside man run the deeper slant instead.) Against zone, that is a
high-low on the hook defender in the middle. Against man coverage, the version drawn below, it
is even better. Two receivers break inside at the same moment, each defender is trying to keep
his own man from getting across his face, and the one defender man coverage usually keeps in the
middle as a helper (the "hole" or "rat" player, built in [Man Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-02-man-coverage.qmd))
faces the same high-low as a zone hook defender: he can drive on the low slant or sink under
the high one, not both. The two paths also cross close to each other, and the defenders have to
fight through that traffic; deliberately running into a defender to block him is a foul once it
happens more than a yard past the line, the [rub route](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd) question
settled in the next chapter.[^opi]

[**Hitch-seam**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hitch-seam): the outside receiver runs a
hitch (five or six yards, stop, turn back to the quarterback) and the inside receiver runs a
seam straight up the field. It is a high-low on the flat defender. Against Cover 3 that
defender is usually coached to *carry* a slot receiver who goes vertical, running up the field
with him until the deep defender takes over, which is exactly why the hitch underneath him is
usually the throw. The seam is the punishment if he doesn't carry: it also threatens the deep
middle safety, who can't take a seam on both sides of the field. Offenses keep him honest by
running seams from both slots, or by having the quarterback look the safety off (stare at one
seam to pull him there) before throwing.

Seven concepts, and notice how few ideas they really contain. Five of them (slant-flat, stick,
snag, double slants and hitch-seam) pick one defender, put two receivers on opposite sides of him
(above and below, or inside and outside), and ask the quarterback to watch that one man and throw
to the one he doesn't take. Spacing does the same thing to the whole underneath coverage at once,
with the quarterback choosing a half of the field before the snap. The speed out skips the
post-snap read entirely: it beats one cornerback's alignment. In every case the quarterback's eyes
are on one player or one alignment, which is why he can run the quick game at full speed.

## Beating press: the receiver's side

Everything so far assumed the receivers get into their routes on time. The defense's
most direct answer to the quick game is to make sure they don't. In
[**press**](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd) coverage, a cornerback
lines up right on the receiver, a yard or so away, and tries to jam him at the snap: punch him,
reroute him, knock him off his path. Its opposite, off coverage, is a defender who starts
five to ten yards away and gives ground ([Coverage Fundamentals](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd)
covers both from the defender's side).

Press attacks the quick game where it lives: the timing. A slant that should break at three
steps breaks at five because the receiver spent two of them fighting through a jam, and the
quarterback, whose back foot has already landed, is left holding the ball with a rush
closing in. That is why press and the quick game are a matched pair in every game plan: the
defense presses to wreck the rhythm, and the offense answers with receivers who can beat press
quickly and routes that use the press defender's own position against him.

The rules frame the fight. Within five yards of the line of scrimmage, an NFL defender may
contact a receiver in front of him; beyond five yards, until the ball is thrown, contact that
impedes the receiver is illegal contact or defensive holding.[^chuck] Either foul costs the
defense five yards and gives the offense an automatic first down, which on third-and-8 is a
gift. So press is a five-yard fight, and the receiver's goal is to get through those five yards on his path and on time.
Here is how he does it, from the receiver's side of the ball.

### Release: getting off the line

A [**release**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-release-vs-press) is a receiver's first
moves off the line against a pressing defender: footwork to make the defender commit, and
hands to keep the defender's hands off him. The defender wants to get his hands on the
receiver's chest and mirror him; the receiver wants to make him move first, then go the other
way.

The inside and outside releases are mirror images of one idea: **make the defender declare
first.** Attack one side hard enough that he has to move his feet or reach to stop it, then go
to the other side. The hands matter as much as the feet: receivers swipe the defender's hands
down, chop at his wrists or rip an arm through under his, to keep him off the chest. A defender
who lands a two-hand jam controls the receiver; one who whiffs has to turn and chase.

Which release a receiver uses is not his whim. On a quick route, the route decides. A
three-step slant *needs* an inside release, a fade or go route an outside one, because there is
no time to go one way and come back. (On longer routes there is, which is why panel 3 shows a
receiver releasing outside and breaking inside: the stem buys the time.) That's why the pre-snap
read includes the press corner's leverage: a corner pressing with inside leverage is daring the
receiver to win inside, so the quarterback may prefer the fade or a quick out to that side, and
the slant to the other.

A corner pressing **head-up**, square in front of the receiver, hasn't given a side away; he
plans to mirror whichever way the receiver goes. The receiver's answer is to make him declare
anyway: a quick flurry of short, choppy steps in place, or a jab one way and then the other,
until the corner's hips or hands commit, and then a release to the side he left. Against a
patient head-up corner that takes an extra beat, so quarterbacks often treat that matchup as a
coin flip and look for a better one on the other side.

### Stem and stack: setting up the break

Once he is off the line, the receiver still has to get open at the top of the route. The
[**stem**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stem) is the part of the route between the
release and the break, and good receivers treat it as a weapon rather than a run-up. By
aiming the stem at one of the defender's shoulders, the receiver tells him what the route
"is": run at his outside shoulder at full speed and the defender has to worry about the go
route and turn his hips to run, which makes a break inside much harder for him to match.

Against a defender trailing in man coverage, the receiver also wants to
[**stack**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stacking-a-defender) him: get directly in
front of him, on his line, so the defender is behind the receiver and can't see or reach the
ball without going through him. A stacked defender can't undercut a throw, can't play the
receiver's hands, and has to guess which way the break will go. The best route runners win
most of their battles here, in the yard or two between "released" and "broken," and that's
why coaches say a route is won before the break, not at it.

### The break and the catch point

The **break** is the cut itself, and its quality decides how much separation the receiver
has when the ball arrives. A sharp break (sink the hips, plant, explode the other way)
creates space against a defender who is mirroring. A rounded break keeps speed, as in the
speed out, and works against a defender who is backing up. Either way, on a quick throw the
ball is usually already in the air.

Then comes the **catch point**: the moment the ball and the receiver's hands meet. If the
release, stem and break were good, it's an easy catch with the defender a step or two away.
If not, it's a
[**contested catch**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-contested-catch): a catch made with a
defender close enough to touch the ball or the receiver's hands. FTN's charters flagged about
14% of 2025 targets as contested; only about 42% of those were caught, against about 71% of
the rest.[^contested] The quick game is designed to avoid contested catches: a well-run
slant-flat or stick throws to the receiver who is *not* covered. When a quick throw becomes a
contested catch, usually against press-man coverage with no open receiver, the offense is
relying on a receiver who can win at the catch point, and on a quarterback willing to throw
him the ball anyway. Throws placed where only the receiver can reach them, like the
[back-shoulder throw](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd),
are how good pairs make those catches more likely.

### The double move: punishing the defender who guesses right

The quick game creates its own counter. A cornerback who has watched film of an offense
throwing slant after slant and hitch after hitch learns to sit on those routes, and to jump
them the instant the receiver breaks. That is exactly the defender a
[**double move**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-double-move) is built for. The
receiver fakes a quick route, the quarterback often pump-fakes (starts his throwing motion
without letting go) as if throwing it, and when the defender drives on the fake, the receiver
turns up the field behind him. The common forms are named for their two parts: slant-and-go (the
[sluggo](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)), out-and-up, hitch-and-go, the stutter-go (a fake
stop), and the stick-nod, in which the stick runner fakes settling and then breaks up the field,
the counter to a flat defender who has learned to drive on the stick.

The double move is the quick game's insurance policy: without it, a defense could squeeze the
short routes harder every week; with it, every corner who jumps a slant risks a long touchdown.
The cost is time. A double move takes three seconds or more, so offenses tend to call it with an
extra blocker, after they have thrown the short version often enough to bait the defender.

## Quick screens: now and bubble

The quick game has two close cousins that aren't really passes in the usual sense. Both are
screens, throws to a receiver behind or at the line of scrimmage with teammates blocking in
front of him, and both are thrown the instant the ball is snapped. (Slower screens to running
backs and tight ends, with linemen releasing to block, are in
[Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens](04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd).)

A [**now screen**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-now-screen) goes to an outside receiver.
He takes a step back (or none) and catches the ball a second after the snap, while the
receiver inside him blocks the nearest defender. Teams call versions of it a
[smoke screen](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-smoke-screen) or a
[quick screen](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-quick-screen); the names vary by playbook
(some use "smoke" for the version with no blocker at all), but the idea is the same.

The now screen exists to punish one thing: **a defender playing far off the ball.** An
eight-yard cushion is eight yards the defender has to cover before he can make a tackle, and
a receiver who catches the ball at the snap gets to spend those yards running instead. Many
offenses attach the now screen to ordinary plays as an extra option (coaches say they *tag* it
on), so that the quarterback, seeing the cornerback backed up eight yards, can throw it as a free
five yards instead of running the called play. The ball comes out at once for a rules reason too:
the receivers who block for it may not block a defender more than a yard past the line before the
pass is thrown, the same one-yard limit that governs rubs.

The [**bubble screen**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bubble-screen) is the inside
version. A slot receiver drifts a step or two back and then out toward the sideline, a path
that looks like a bubble when you draw it, and catches the ball already running, while the
receivers outside him turn and block.

Coaches who throw these screens on almost every snap, as many college offenses do and some
NFL offenses do, often teach the decision with three words: **numbers, leverage, grass.**

- **Numbers:** count the defenders outside the box on one side and compare them with the
  offense's players there. Three against two is a screen. This is the
  [box count](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) seen from
  the other side: every defender a defense puts in the box to stop the run is one fewer
  outside it.
- **Leverage:** can the blockers get between their defenders and the ball carrier? A
  defender lined up inside, near the ball, is easy to block from the outside; one lined up
  wide is not.
- **Grass:** how much space is there between the ball carrier and the nearest unblocked
  defender? A safety twelve yards deep is twelve yards of grass.

That is why quick screens are often thought of as part of the run game, and why they are so
often packaged with runs. If the defense puts a seventh or eighth man in the box to stop the
run, someone outside the box has left, and the screen to that side gets better. When the
quarterback decides between the run and the screen *after* the snap, by reading a defender, the
play becomes a [run-pass option](04-06-rpos.qmd), and the bubble attached to a run is one of the
most common RPOs in football ([bubble RPO](04-06-rpos.qmd)).

One rule detail makes the bubble unusual. Because it is often thrown sideways or slightly
backward, a bubble that is thrown behind the receiver is a backward pass, and a backward
pass that hits the ground is a live ball, not an incompletion: either team can recover it.[^backward]
That's why you sometimes see a defender scoop up a dropped bubble and run the other way, and
why offenses want the throw to be clearly forward or clearly caught.

## The answer to press and blitz

Now put the chapter together. The two most aggressive things a defense can do against the
pass are to **blitz** (send more rushers than the offense can comfortably block) and to
**press** (jam receivers to destroy the timing). Both are bets that the quarterback won't get
the ball out in time. The quick game is the offense taking that bet.

The arithmetic of a blitz explains why. A [five-man pressure](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd)
sends five rushers. Keep six men in to block (the five linemen and the back) and the offense can
pick up all five with a man to spare. Keep only five and it can still block five rushers on paper,
but only if the protection is aimed at the right five. Protections are set before the snap by
counting the defenders who *might* rush ([Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd)'s
[slide](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slide-protection) and Mike identification). If the line
slides toward two linebackers and one of them drops into coverage while a defender from the other
edge comes, one blocker is left with nobody and one rusher has no blocker at all: a
[free rusher](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-free-rusher). Send six against five and somebody is
free no matter what. Either way the protection's rule is that the free man belongs to the
quarterback. He is "hot": the ball has to come out before he arrives, on a
[hot route](04-02-pass-protection.qmd) or a [sight adjustment](04-02-pass-protection.qmd) aimed at
the area the blitzer just left.

Behind the blitz, the coverage is thin. It is often man coverage, pressed, with one safety deep
or none, or a [fire zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fire-zone) (three deep defenders and
three underneath, built in [Zone Blitz and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd)).
In either case the blitzer's old spot is empty. A quick throw attacks every part of that: it beats
the free rusher to the quarterback, and it goes to a receiver who is alone in coverage or running
into the hole the blitzer left.

::: {#cell-fig-pressure .cell execution_count=14}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def pressure_play():
    off = spread(rb_w=1.5)
    dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.4, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"),
           D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -4.0, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 2.2, 0.6, "M"),
           D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -10.5, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -15.6, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.2, 15.6, "CB"),
           D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 8.6, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
    # a five-man slide right: LT and LG take the two linemen in front of them, C/RG/RT step to their right
    for k, (dd, ww) in (("LT", (-1.3, -1.4)), ("LG", (-1.0, 0.2)), ("C", (-1.0, 1.3)), ("RG", (-1.0, 1.0)),
                        ("RT", (-1.2, 1.2))):
        p.block(k, pts=[(dd, ww)], speed=4.0)
        p.block(k, pts=[(-0.4, 0.0)], speed=0.6)
    for k in ("WDE", "WDT", "SDT", "SDE"):           # the four linemen rush and engage them
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=4.0)
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-0.4, 0.0)], speed=0.6)
    p.dropback(2.0, speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "NB", (-6.4, -1.4), kind="rush", speed=6.3, delay=0.2, via=[(1.0, -7.2)])
    p.route("RB", r.path((0.5, 4.5), (1.4, 8.5), (5.0, 10.5), (6.0, 11.5)), side=1)
    p.man("MIKE", "RB")
    # X: a jab outside against the press corner, an inside release through his hands, then the stem and slant
    p.route("X", [(0, 0), (0.2, 0.8)], speed=2.4)
    p.route("X", [(0, 0), (2.2, -1.6)], speed=4.4)                 # hand-fight through the jam
    p.route("X", [(0, 0), (3.4, -0.2)], speed=4.4)                 # re-accelerate up the stem
    p.route("X", [(0, 0), (4.2, -5.8), (5.4, -8.0)], speed=6.6)    # the break and the slant
    p.route("H", r.seam(18.0))
    p.man("WILL", "H")
    p.route("Y", r.hitch(6.0))
    p.man("SS", "Y")
    p.route("Z", r.go(16.0))
    p.man("RCB", "Z")
    p.drop("FS", (14.0, 0.0))
    p.pass_to("X", t=2.1)
    trail(p, "LCB", "X", jab=(1.3, -16.2), off=(-0.9, -0.9), t_on=1.1)  # bites on the jab, then chases from behind
    return p
```

Quick game against a five-man pressure (simulated tracking in the Big Data Bowl format). The defense shows press-man coverage with one deep safety (Cover 1), with the Mike linebacker (M) walked up over the center as a possible sixth rusher. The running back releases into a route, so the offense has five blockers, and the line slides right toward the Mike: the left tackle takes the end in front of him, the left guard the tackle, and the center, right guard and right tackle step right. At the snap the Mike drops out to cover the back, so the center has nobody, and the slot defender ($, ringed in orange) blitzes off the offense's left edge, where nobody is left to block him. He is the quarterback's man: hot. X (ringed in green) beats the press cornerback with an inside release, which costs him a beat, and breaks in on a slant into the area the blitzer left. The ball is out 2.1 seconds after the snap, a beat before the blitzer gets there.
:::
:::


Three details in that play are worth slowing down for. First, the quarterback knew before the
snap where the ball was likely to go. Pressed corners with a single safety deep is a classic
pressure look, and the slot defender creeping toward the line told him which area might empty.
His pre-snap plan was "if the $ comes, the ball goes to X, inside, right now." Second, he
confirmed it with one look after the snap. The $ might have been bluffing, showing a blitz and
then backing out into coverage; the moment he crossed the line of scrimmage, the plan was on.
Had he backed out, the quarterback would simply have run the play's normal read. Third, the
slant was the right route for the press cornerback's leverage: he lined up on X's outside, so an
inside release was the release X could win. That release cost X a beat (against off coverage
the same slant would come out around 1.2 to 1.5 seconds), which is why this ball left at 2.1:
still on time for X, still ahead of the blitz.
