The chart puts a number on the trade.[^rushepa] Against a standard four-man rush, a quick
throw was worth about an eighth of a point more than a slower outcome. Against five or more
rushers, the gap roughly doubles: quick throws gained about +0.23 expected points per
dropback, while everything slower, with the sacks that a blitz produces, averaged about
-0.10. A blitz is a coin flip the defense is offering, and a quarterback who gets the ball out
before the extra rusher arrives wins the flip far more often than he loses it.

So why do defenses blitz at all, on about one dropback in four? Because pooled over every
outcome, the bet is roughly even. In 2025, dropbacks against five or more rushers averaged about
+0.05 expected points for the offense, against +0.04 for four or fewer: a hair worse for the
defense, within the noise, but with more sacks (about 7.8% of dropbacks against 6.0%). And
blitzes come more often on third down (about 30% of dropbacks, against 25% on first and second),
where forcing a short throw that falls short of the line to gain is a win in itself. The blitz is a variance play: it produces sacks
and hurried incompletions, and it gives up the quick completion into the space it vacated. That is
why blitz-happy defenses spend so much effort disguising when and where the pressure will come
from ([Blitz and Man Pressure](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd) does the math
from the defense's side; [Zone Blitz and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd)
the disguises).

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game, the blitz is a button you press to make the other player panic. In the NFL,
a quarterback who sees six defenders at the line is usually not panicking; his offense has
spent the week on what to do when that happens. Every quick concept is installed with its blitz
answer: which receiver becomes hot (the ball goes to him at once, often on a shortened version
of his route) if a particular defender comes, which routes become sight adjustments, and which
rusher, if any, the protection call leaves unblocked. The real contest is whether the defense
can *hide* the blitz until it's too late to adjust, or show one and not bring it. That's why
the pre-snap dance of defenders walking up and backing out, covered in
[The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd), matters so much.
:::

## Film room: three offenses that lived on it

The quick game is in every playbook, but a few offenses built their identity on it. Each of
the three below shows a different reason to.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: New Orleans Saints 2017–2019"}
**The quick game as accuracy.** Late in Drew Brees's career, the engine of Sean Payton's offense
(Payton was head coach 2006–2021, Brees the quarterback 2006–2020) was the short, on-time throw.
Brees broke the NFL's single-season completion-percentage record in 2017 (72.0%) and broke it
again in 2018 (74.4%).[^brees] In 2019, among quarterbacks with 300 or more attempts, he had the
second-fastest average time to throw and one of the shortest average throws (about 6.5 yards),
and Michael Thomas set the single-season receptions record with 149, about seven in ten of them on
throws that traveled less than ten yards in the air.[^thomas]

**What to notice on the tape:** the ball leaving on Brees's last step, again and again, and
Thomas getting inside the cornerback on the slant, then shielding the ball with his body at the
catch point.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: New England Patriots 2007–2012"}
**The quick game as an option tree.** The Tom Brady–era Patriots ran it through a small, quick
slot receiver. Wes Welker caught 112 passes in 2007, 123 in 2009 and 122 in 2011, leading the
league three times in five years,[^welker] most of them within a few yards of the line, many on
option routes in which he read his defender's leverage and broke away from it, the same rule the
stick route uses. Brady's clock stayed fast long after: in 2022, at 45, he had the fastest
average time to throw of any regular starter.[^brady]

**What to notice on the tape:** Welker inside, a defender over him trying to guess his break,
and Brady throwing as Welker turned his head, before the break had finished.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Kansas City Chiefs 2022–2024"}
**The quick game as an adaptation.** In 2018, Patrick Mahomes's first season as the starter, the
Chiefs threw deep more than almost anyone, with Tyreek Hill as the threat. Defenses adjusted
first. Their throws were already getting shorter in 2019, 2020 and 2021, with Hill still on the
roster, as opponents played two deep safeties to take away the big play: by 2021, Kansas City saw
a two-high shell on about 46% of its dropbacks, third-most in the league.[^kc2high] Then Hill was
traded to Miami in March 2022,[^hill] and over the next three seasons Andy Reid rebuilt the
offense around shorter throws to Travis Kelce and a rotating cast of receivers. By 2023 and 2024
the Chiefs' average throw was the second-shortest in the league (the chart after this box shows
the whole slide). They won the Super Bowl after the
2022 and 2023 seasons anyway.


**What to notice on the tape:** Kelce, lined up in the slot or as the innermost receiver of
trips, running a stick or an option route at five to eight yards and settling between two zone
defenders, with Mahomes throwing as he turns. Nearly three of every four of Kelce's targets in
2022 traveled less than ten yards in the air.[^kc] For one clip, find Super Bowl LVII (February
12, 2023, against Philadelphia): in the fourth quarter, on third-and-goal from the 4, Skyy Moore
went in motion, reversed and ran to the flat, and Mahomes threw it to him for a touchdown
1.7 seconds after the snap, against a defense charted as Cover 0 with seven rushers. The
Chiefs had scored on the same motion play, run to the other side to Kadarius Toney, less than three
minutes of game clock earlier.[^sb57] That's the quick game at its purest: everybody coming, nobody deep, and the ball
gone before it matters.

The 2025 point on the chart below matters too: with a different set of receivers, the Chiefs' depth
went back to about the league median. The quick game here was never a fixed identity; it was a
great offense taking what the defenses of those years left underneath.
:::

::: {#cell-fig-kc-adot .cell execution_count=16}

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: one-two-throw"}
**Before the snap**

- **The corners.** Off or pressed? Inside or outside the receiver? A corner seven yards off
  with outside leverage is inviting a slant or a now screen; a pressed corner is daring the
  receiver to beat him off the line.
- **The slot defender.** Where is the man between the slot receiver and the box? He is the
  read on almost every quick concept to that side. If he walks up toward the line, think
  blitz, and think quick throw.
- **Count outside the box.** Three receivers against two defenders on one side, with the
  safety far away, is a screen waiting to happen.

**At the snap: the stopwatch.** Count "one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two" from the snap. If the
ball is gone before you finish "two," you just watched the quick game working as designed. Count a
dozen dropbacks in a game and you'll find that roughly half of them are out before
"two-and-a-half."

**At the snap: watch the linemen.** Three plays come out in about a second, and the linemen tell
them apart. On a quick throw they set to pass-block, short and aggressive, and stay at the line.
On a run-pass option they fire forward as if blocking a run. On a now or bubble screen the
*receivers* near the ball turn and block.

**After the throw**

- On the replay, find the one defender between the two receivers on the side the ball went.
  Did he widen, sink or sit? The ball went to the receiver he didn't take.
- When the defense blitzes, watch where the ball goes. Usually it goes quickly to the area the
  blitzer came from.

**For your prediction log** ([How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)):
before each third-and-short-to-medium, write *quick* or *not quick*, and the side you expect,
based on the corners' leverage. Then time the throw.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: pick a side"}

::: {#cell-fig-predict-side .cell execution_count=17}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = spread()
dfn = cover3(nb_side=-1, extra={"RCB": (1.3, 14.2), "SS": (3.5, 12.0), "NB": (5.0, -7.0)})
p = Play(off, dfn, los=45, to_go=6)
protect(p)
p.dropback(1.5)
for k in ("X", "Z"):
    p.route(k, r.slant(stem=3.0, length=9.0))
for k in ("H", "Y"):
    p.route(k, r.path((1.0, 1.8), (3.0, 10.0)))
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-25.0, 25.0), window=(-8.5, 15.5))
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Second-and-6. The offense has called slant-flat to both sides (outside receiver on a slant, slot receiver to the flat) and left the choice of side to the quarterback.](04-03-quick-game_files/figure-html/fig-predict-side-output-1.svg){#fig-predict-side}
:::
:::


**Which side should the quarterback pick, and which defender does he watch after the snap?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The left side, reading the slot defender ($).** Run through the pre-snap read on each side.

On the **right**, both routes are in trouble before the snap. The cornerback is pressed with
inside leverage, sitting right where Z's slant wants to go, so Z has to beat a jam *and* get
across the cornerback's face; and the safety has already widened to the flat, standing where
Y's flat route ends. One defender is in each receiver's path.

On the **left**, the cornerback is seven yards off and outside X, which concedes the slant
(away from leverage), and the slot defender is inside H, the one man who has to choose between
the two routes. That's the slant-flat picture from earlier in the chapter. After the snap the
quarterback watches only the $: if he widens with H, throw the slant; if he sits, throw the flat.

Doesn't the right side have its own answer? A corner pressing with inside leverage invites an
outside release and the fade, and Z might win it. But the fade isn't in this call, and even when
it is, it's a lower-percentage throw against a corner who is right on top of the receiver. On the
left, the play works exactly as designed, with two receivers against one defender and an easy
read. The quarterback takes the side where the concept he called is already winning.

This is why offenses call a quick concept to both sides. The defense has to give something
away somewhere, and the quarterback's pre-snap job is to find where.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: six at the line"}

::: {#cell-fig-predict-zero .cell execution_count=18}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = spread()
dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.4, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"),
       D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 1.9, -2.3, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 1.9, 0.8, "M"),
       D("NB", "NB", 3.0, -8.6, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 3.0, 8.6, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 6.0, 0.6, "FS"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 1.3, -13.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.3, 13.8, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=50, to_go=5)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-25.0, 25.0), window=(-8.5, 12.5))
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Third-and-5, just before the snap. The offense has five linemen, and a running back who can stay in to block or go out for a pass.](04-03-quick-game_files/figure-html/fig-predict-zero-output-1.svg){#fig-predict-zero}
:::
:::


**Count the threat. What kind of throw does the offense want, how fast, and where?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A hot throw, out in about a second and a half, and away from the cornerbacks' leverage.**
Count first. Nobody is deeper than about six yards: this is a "zero" look, with no deep safety at
all ([Cover 0](../06-pass-coverage/06-02-man-coverage.qmd)). Zero lets the defense put a man on
every receiver and send everyone else. With five receivers out, that is six rushers against five
blockers. If the back stays in to block, his defender can come too: seven rushers against six
blockers. Either way one rusher is free, and nobody can hold the ball. That is the
[Cover 0 blitz](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd) bet: the defense is wagering
that the ball can't come out in time.

Now look at the cornerbacks. Both are pressed and both are a yard *inside* their receivers. That
is the leverage rule at work: with no safety anywhere, the corner has no help inside, so he
protects the middle and uses the sideline as his help. The slant, the quick game's favorite throw,
is the route he is sitting on. So the ball goes away from his leverage, outside. Two answers fit:

- **The outside receivers' fade or back-shoulder throw.** With no safety behind the corner, a
  receiver who wins outside off the line is one catch from a touchdown, and the quarterback can
  throw it as soon as the receiver clears the jam. It's not a high-percentage throw (a pressed
  corner is right on the receiver), which is why it isn't the answer every time.
- **The hot route into the space a blitzer leaves.** Some of the defenders crowding the line
  will cover and some will rush. The receiver whose nearest defender rushes is hot: he breaks
  into the space that defender just left, and the ball goes there at once.

Which side? The side the protection call says the free rusher is coming from, because that is
where the hot receiver is and where the quarterback has the least time. A now screen is a poor
choice: the cornerback is standing a yard away, so there is no cushion to run into.

For a real one, see the Super Bowl LVII touchdown to Skyy Moore in the Chiefs film room above:
seven rushers, Cover 0, ball out in 1.7 seconds to the flat.

lanes. That is exactly why the throw is a *read* of where the extra defenders went, not just a
reflex ([Zone Blitz and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd)).

**The defense has loaded the box to stop the run. What quick throw does that invite, and why?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A quick screen to the trips side: a bubble to H, or a now screen to Z.** Start by counting.
The box (roughly the area between the offensive tackles, out to about five yards deep) holds
seven defenders: four linemen, two linebackers and a safety. Outside it on the right there are
only the cornerback and the $. Then run the three questions:

- **Numbers:** on the right, outside the box, the offense has three players (Y, H and Z) and the
  defense two. The safety who would usually be the third defender out there is standing beside the
  linebackers, in the box. That's the trade the defense made: an extra run defender inside, one
  fewer pass defender outside.
- **Leverage:** the cornerback and the $ are both off and roughly over their receivers, so
  the blockers start in the right place: Z can turn the cornerback out toward the sideline, and
  Y, starting inside the $, can block him from the inside while H runs between them.
- **Grass:** both are about seven yards off, and the nearest help, the deep safety, is
  fourteen yards away in the middle of the field. A bubble caught at the snap is five yards
  gained before anyone can touch it.

A run into the middle would face seven defenders with five linemen to block them (six if a
receiver comes in to help): the defense has the numbers inside. The
quick screen is how the offense "runs" outside the box instead, and it's why so many offenses
attach a bubble to their running plays ([Run-Pass Options](04-06-rpos.qmd)).
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- The **quick game** is the passing game's fast lane: a short drop, short routes and a rhythm
  throw, out in about **2.5 seconds or less**. It is roughly half of what NFL offenses throw.
- It exists for **three jobs**: beat the rush with the clock, keep the offense **on schedule**
  with high-percentage throws, and **stretch the run game sideways** by getting the ball to fast
  players in space. It trades depth for certainty and needs yards after the catch and a deep
  threat to keep the bargain.
- Most quick concepts put **two receivers on opposite sides of one defender**, high and low
  (slant-flat, hitch-seam, double slants) or inside and outside (stick), or both (snag's
  triangle), and the quarterback throws to the one that defender doesn't take. Spacing stretches
  the whole underneath coverage; the speed out beats one cornerback's alignment.
- Most of the decision is made **before the snap**: read the defender's **leverage**, cushion
  and help, and throw away from leverage.
- **Press** is the defense's answer to the quick game's timing; the receiver's answer is the
  **release, stem, stack and break**, and the **double move** punishes a defender who jumps the
  short route.
- **Now and bubble screens** punish soft and outnumbered alignments (numbers, leverage, grass).
  Against **the blitz**, the free rusher is the quarterback's, and the ball that comes out fast,
  into the space the blitzer left, is worth the most.

import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
player_play = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/player_play.csv")

quick = plays[(plays["timeToThrow"] < 2.5) & (plays["passResult"] == "C")]
slants = player_play.loc[player_play["routeRan"] == "SLANT", ["gameId", "playId"]].drop_duplicates()

one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
